notes_theme = theme_minimal(base_size = 14, base_family = "Source Sans 3")
theme_set(notes_theme)

regression_panel <- function(formula, scat.formula = NULL, data, xlab, ylab) {
  mod <- lm(formula, data = data)
  
  aug <- augment(mod)
  
  plot_fit <- makeFun(mod)
  
  if(is.null(scat.formula)) {
    orig_data <- gf_point(formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300")
  } else {
    orig_data <- gf_point(scat.formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300") 
  }
  
  orig_data <- orig_data %>% gf_fun(plot_fit(x) ~ x, color = "#f15a31")
  
  resid_plot <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Standardized residuals") %>%
    gf_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "#f15a31")
  
  qq_plot <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, xlab = "N(0,1) quantiles", ylab = "Standardized residuals", color = "#003300") %>%
    gf_qqline(color = "#f15a31")
  
  (orig_data | resid_plot | qq_plot)
}

## Why doesn't `glm` work?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true
model2 <- glm(Removed ~ distance + morph + distance * morph, 
              data = moths, 
              family = "binomial")
```


## Binomial response

- $Y_i$: the **number** of moths removed (i.e. "success") on each tree for each morph

- We will **assume** each trial (success/failure) is independent

::: callout-note
## Binomial distribution

The sum of independent and identically distributed success/failure trials follows a Binomial(n, p) distribution.

- Theoretical mean: $E(Y) = np$
- Theoretical variance: $Var(Y) = np(1-p)$
- A binary response is the special case where $n=1$ 

:::

## Binomial logistic regression

$$\pi_i = P(success | x_1, ..., x_p)$$

Log-odds scale: 

$$\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \log (\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... + \beta_p x_p = \eta_i$$

Probability scale: 

$$\pi_i = \dfrac{e^{\eta_i}}{1 + e^{\eta_i}}= \dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}}}$$

## 

This approach required calculating the empirical log-odds "by hand" and adding to the dataset.  Alternatively, we can fit with `glm()` using the `weights` argument

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true
model3 <- glm(Removed/Placed ~ distance + morph + distance*morph, 
              weights = Placed,
              data = moths, 
              family = "binomial")
```

```{r}
tidy(model3)
```

::: footer
The estimates are slightly different due to different assumptions (eg $\varepsilon$)
:::

## Binomial model assumptions

- **Binomial counts**: Y is number of successes in $n$ trials

- **Independence**: observations are independent

- **Linearity**: the log odds is a linear function of the predictors

- **Variance structure**: the variance of a binomial random variable is $n \pi (1 - \pi)$

    $\Longrightarrow$ so the variance of $Y_i$ is $n_i \pi_i (1 - \pi_i)$ (not constant!)
    
## Pearson residuals

$${\rm Pres}_i = \dfrac{Y_i - n_i \widehat{\pi}_i}{\sqrt{n_i \widehat{\pi}_i (1 - \widehat{\pi}_i)}}$$

For large enough $n_i$, Pearson residuals tend to behave like they come from $N(0,1)$

How to use?

- Plot against fitted values, predictors

- Check for curvature, outliers

## Pearson residuals

```{r}
p1 <- ggResidpanel::resid_panel(model3, type = "pearson", plots = c("resid", "qq"), smoother = TRUE)
p2 <- ggResidpanel::resid_xpanel(model3, type = "pearson", smoother = TRUE, nrow = 1)

p1 / p2
```

## Pearson $\chi^2$

::: medium

Pearson's $\chi^2$ statistic can be used to assess the **overall fit** of a binomial logistic regression model



Observed Count | Predicted P(Success) | True P(Success) | Predicted Count 
:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:
$Y_i$ | $\widehat{\pi}_i$ | $\pi_i$ | $m_i \widehat\pi_i$


**Pearson $\chi^2$:** $X^2 = \sum \dfrac{(Y_i - m_i\widehat{\pi}_i)^2}{m_i\widehat{\pi}_i (1 - \widehat{\pi}_i)} = \sum {\rm Pres}_i^2$

:::

::: small

$X^2$ is small when the predicted counts are close to the observed counts (good), and large when they are far away (bad) 

<br>

$X^2 \overset{\cdot}{\sim} \chi^2$ with $\text{d.f.}= n-(p+1)$, **if** the model is correct and all $m_i$ are large enough (>5)

$n =$ \# of binomial observations (\# of proportions, not # of moths)
:::




## Goodness-of-fit test

<div style="float: right; clear: right; margin: 10px;">(the model is adequate)</div>

:::{style="font-size:0.9em"}
H<sub>0</sub>: ${\rm logit}(\pi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$
:::

<div style="float: right; clear: right; margin: 10px;">(the model is inadequate)</div>

:::{style="font-size:0.9em"}
H<sub>a</sub>: ${\rm logit}(\pi_i) = \alpha_i$
:::


<br>

::: medium

```{r}
#| echo: true
X2 <- sum(residuals(model3, type = "pearson")^2)
X2
df.residual(model3)
```

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true
1 - pchisq(X2, 10)
```

:::

<br>

:::{style="font-size:0.5em"}
Note: This test is *only valid for the binomial logistic regression*, it is not valid for binary logistic regression.
:::

## Goodness-of-fit test

```{r}
lambda <- sum(residuals(model3, type = "pearson")^2)   # observed Pearson X2
df <- 10          # degrees of freedom

gf_dist("chisq", df = df, geom = "area",
        fill = ~ (x > qchisq(.95, df)), xlim = c(0, 25),
        show.legend = FALSE) |>
  gf_vline(xintercept = lambda, linetype = 2) |>
  gf_labs(x = "Chi-square statistic", y = "Density",
          title = paste0("p-value = ", round(1 - pchisq(lambda, df), 4))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("gray85", "darkorange"))

```

## 

::: medium
|                             | Binary logistic                                                                                       | Binomial logistic                                                                                                                       |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Response                    | A single 0/1 outcome      | The number of successes $Y_i$ out of $n_i$ trials                               |
| `glm()` response            | `y ~ x`, with `y` coded 0/1                                                                           | `y/n ~ x, weights = n`                                                                                |
| Residual plots              | Empirical logit plots (bin $x$ first) and Pearson residuals with a smoother (two bands)| Empirical logit plots (no binning) and Pearson residuals; $\approx N(0,1)$ when the $n_i$ are large                    |
| Goodness-of-fit test valid? | No ($n_i = 1$)                                                                                        | Yes, if the $n_i$ are large enough       |

-   Binomial logistic regression models the **probability** of success for each row, using the same logit link as binary logistic regression.
-   The variance of $Y_i$ is $n_i\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$, so it depends on $\pi_i$.

:::
